title: Searching: grep and find
lead: grep searches lines inside files, while find searches for files and directories in a directory tree. Combine them to inspect logs and project files quickly.
objectives: Find files by name and type with `find`.
Use search results with pipes and redirection.

sections.title: Search file contents with grep
body: `grep PATTERN FILE` prints matching lines. The pattern can be plain text or a regular expression. Use `-i` to ignore case, `-n` to show line numbers, `-v` to select non-matching lines and `-c` to count matching lines.
`grep` can also read text from a pipe when no filename is given. This lets you filter long output with `command | grep pattern`.

commands.what: Shows line numbers alongside matching lines.
commands.where: When locating a match in a file.
commands.why: Makes it easier to find and inspect the result.

commands.where: When log messages use different capitalization.

commands.what: Shows lines that do not match the pattern.
commands.where: When excluding unwanted lines from results.
commands.why: Filters the inverse of a match.

commands.what: Prints the number of matching lines.
commands.where: When counting events in a log.
commands.why: Gives a total without printing every line.

sections.tip: Pass the pattern and filename as separate arguments. Quote a search string that contains special characters.

sections.title: Search the file system with find
body: `find START ...` searches downwards from the given directory. `-name` selects a name pattern, `-type f` selects regular files and `-type d` selects directories. Quote filename patterns so the shell does not expand `*` before find receives it.

`find` can search by more than name, and its output can be piped to another command. `locate` searches a prebuilt filename index; it is fast, but newly created files may not be indexed yet. Starting from a focused directory avoids scanning unrelated system paths.

commands.what: Searches by name in a directory tree.
commands.where: When you know a filename or extension inside a project.
When you need to distinguish files from directories.
commands.why: Limits results to one kind of filesystem object.

commands.where: When locating folders inside a project.
commands.why: Keeps directory names separate from filenames.

commands.what: Searches an indexed database of filenames quickly.
commands.where: When looking for the path of a known file across the system.
commands.why: It is fast when the index is current; new files may not appear yet.

sections.warn: `find /` can scan the entire system and produce permission warnings. Start with a narrow path such as your project or home directory.

sections.title: Combine searches and save results
body: `grep` and `find` answer different questions: grep finds text inside files, while find locates files by name and path. Save results with `>` or pass them to another filter with `|`.
Inspect search results before changing important files. The commands in this module search and read; redirection creates a report only in your working directory.

commands.what: Searches file contents recursively in a directory.
commands.where: When finding where a setting or word appears in a project.
commands.why: Avoids opening files one by one.

commands.what: Writes paths of matching text files to a list.
commands.where: When you want to inspect search results later.
commands.why: Keeps results in a reusable report.

vm.intro: Read existing text and paths on your own VM. These commands do not change system files; use your home directory when creating a report.

v01.title: Search a log
v01.text: Search a system log for `error`, ignoring case, and paste one matching line.
differs: If that log does not exist, choose a log on your distribution or create `~/lab/app.log` with sample lines.

v02.title: Show line numbers
v02.text: Find the `root` line in `/etc/passwd` and include its line number.
differs: The line number may vary by system; the output should contain `root` with a number before it.

v03.title: Search by filename
differs: The output should contain the full path. `find` takes the starting directory and name as separate arguments.

v04.title: Save results safely
v04.text: Create `lab` in your home directory, make a report listing `.txt` files there, and inspect the report.

blocks.cmd: mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && touch notes.txt readme.txt && find . -type f -name '*.txt' > files.txt && cat files.txt

differs: If the report is empty, check that `cd ~/lab` succeeded and the filenames are correct. Do not search the whole system.

options: Shows matching lines regardless of letter case

q2.q: What does `grep -n` add to its output?
q2.explain: `-n` shows the line number for each match.

q3.q: What does `find project -type f -name '*.txt'` search for?
options: Regular files ending in .txt under project
q3.explain: The starting path is `project`, the type is regular file, and the name pattern ends in `.txt`.

q4.q: Which command searches file contents recursively for `TODO`?
q4.explain: `grep -r` searches file contents recursively in a directory tree.

summary: `grep` searches file contents; `find` locates files and directories in a tree.
`grep -i` ignores case, `-n` shows line numbers, `-v` inverts matches and `-c` counts them.
`find -name` selects a name pattern; `-type f` selects regular files and `-type d` directories.
Quote filename patterns so the shell does not expand `*` before the search.
Start from a narrow directory instead of searching a large tree unnecessarily.

glossary.meaning: A search tool that finds matching lines in text files.

A pattern syntax for matching text.
